title: W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, Read Me First
text:
## No ARIA is Better Than Bad ARIA

The foundational principle of the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) is that incorrect ARIA can do serious harm. Incorrect ARIA misrepresents visual experiences, with potentially devastating effects on their corresponding non-visual experiences. A screen reader user who is told a control is a button when it does nothing, or told a region is a list when it is a table, is worse off than if the ARIA were absent. This is why the guidance is often summarized as: no ARIA is better than bad ARIA.

## Principle 1: A Role Is a Promise

When you apply an ARIA role to an element, you take on responsibility for everything that role implies. Using div role="button" commits you to providing all the keyboard interactions a native button would provide, implemented yourself in JavaScript. ARIA roles do not cause browsers to provide keyboard behaviors or styling the way native HTML elements do. ARIA only changes how assistive technology interprets an element; it changes nothing about the element's actual behavior. So a role is a promise you must keep with scripting: focusability, keyboard operation, state management, and visible focus.

## Principle 2: ARIA Can Both Cloak and Enhance

ARIA functions in two ways. It can override (cloak) the native semantics of an element, or it can enhance (add to) them. The danger of cloaking is that authors can inadvertently override accessibility semantics. For example, applying role="log" to a table hides the tabular nature of the content from assistive technology users, who then lose the row and column relationships they need. Use ARIA deliberately, understanding whether you are replacing meaning or adding it.

## Test Before Production

Testing assistive technology interoperability is essential before using code from the guide in production. The APG examples intentionally do not include workarounds for the many gaps in ARIA support across browser and assistive technology combinations, so implementers must verify real behavior with real assistive technologies rather than assuming the specification is honored everywhere.

title: W3C, Using ARIA (the Rules of ARIA Use)
text:
## First Rule of ARIA Use

If you can use a native HTML element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible, then do so. In other words, reach for button, a, input, select, and the other native elements before you reach for role attributes. The rule acknowledges this is not always possible: an HTML feature may lack the accessibility support you need, a visual design constraint may rule out the native element, or the feature you need may simply not exist in HTML. Absent those exceptions, native first.

## Second Rule of ARIA Use

Do not change native semantics, unless you really have to. The canonical mistake is wrapping a heading in a tab role, for example h2 role="tab", which destroys the heading semantics. The correct pattern nests the heading inside a separate element that carries the role, for example a div role="tab" containing the h2, so both the tab role and the heading survive.

## Third Rule of ARIA Use

All interactive ARIA controls must be usable with the keyboard. If a user can click, tap, drag, drop, slide, or scroll a control with a mouse or touch, they must also be able to navigate to it and operate it with the keyboard, and the control must respond to the expected standard keystrokes for its role.

## Fourth Rule of ARIA Use

Do not use role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element. Doing so lets a keyboard user focus an element that has been removed from the accessibility tree, so they land on nothing, with no announced name, role, or state. Focusable and hidden are contradictory.

## Fifth Rule of ARIA Use

All interactive elements must have an accessible name. An input, button, link, or custom widget with a role but no accessible name is announced only by its role ("button", "edit") with nothing to distinguish it, which is useless to a screen reader user. Provide the name via visible label text, aria-label, aria-labelledby, or an associated label element.

title: MDN Web Docs, Structuring documents (semantic sectioning)
text:
## Semantic Sectioning Elements

HTML provides dedicated semantic elements that communicate the functional purpose of content to browsers, assistive technologies, and developers, rather than generic div elements everywhere. The core sectioning and landmark elements are header, nav, main, article, section, aside, and footer.

header represents introductory content. As a direct child of body it is the global site header; nested inside an article or section it is a header specific to that section. nav contains the major navigation of the page, typically the primary menu; minor or repeated links do not belong in nav. main contains the content unique to this page, and there must be only one main per page, placed directly inside body and not nested inside other sectioning elements. article encloses a self-contained block that makes sense on its own, such as a single blog post, news story, comment, or forum post. section groups a single thematic part or one piece of functionality, and each section should begin with a heading. aside holds content indirectly related to the main content, such as a glossary entry, author biography, related links, or sidebar. footer represents end content such as copyright, contact information, and secondary navigation.

## Why Semantic HTML Matters

Screen readers recognize semantic elements and announce them, so a user can ask to find the main navigation or jump to the main content. Visuals do not tell the whole story: sighted users get color and font size cues, but around 4 to 5 percent of the world population experience some degree of vision loss and roughly 8 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women are colorblind, so structure must be conveyed in markup, not only in appearance. Semantic markup also helps search engines understand page structure and makes code easier to maintain because it reflects meaning.

## Avoid Div Soup

div is a non-semantic block-level wrapper and span is its inline counterpart. Use them only when no semantic element fits, and label them with a class for CSS or JavaScript targeting. Defaulting to a div for every container ("div soup") strips meaning from the document, degrades accessibility, and should be minimized.

## Recommended Page Skeleton

A well-structured page nests a global header, a nav for primary navigation, a single main containing one or more article elements (each with internal section subdivisions and a heading), an aside for related content, and a global footer. The hr element denotes a thematic break between paragraph-level content, and br forces a line break within text such as an address or poem.

title: web.dev (Google), Web Vitals
text:
## The Three Core Web Vitals

Core Web Vitals are the subset of Web Vitals that apply to every web page and measure three distinct facets of real-world user experience: loading, interactivity, and visual stability. Each metric is measurable in the field and reflects a critical user-centric outcome.

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading performance. A good LCP is within 2.5 seconds of when the page first starts loading. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness to interactions. A good INP is 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability. A good CLS is 0.1 or less.

## The 75th Percentile Rule

To ensure the experience is good for most visits, the recommended target for each metric must be met at the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop devices. A page passes the Core Web Vitals assessment only when it meets the good target at the 75th percentile for all three metrics. Measuring at the 75th percentile, rather than the average or median, means you are optimizing for the slower quarter of real user sessions, not just the typical case, which is where poor experiences hide.

## Field Data and an Evolving Set

Core Web Vitals are measured in the field (real user monitoring), not only in the lab, because they reflect real-world experience; lab tools can approximate LCP and CLS but interactivity metrics like INP need real interactions. The set is not fixed: it evolves over time as measurement improves. INP graduated to a Core Web Vital and replaced First Input Delay (FID) as the responsiveness metric in March 2024, because INP measures the latency of all interactions across the visit rather than only the first. A UI engineer should treat the three current metrics as the shipping bar but expect the specific metrics to change as the web platform matures.

title: web.dev (Google), Optimize Largest Contentful Paint
text:
## The LCP Target and Its Four Subparts

Sites should strive for an LCP of 2.5 seconds or less for at least 75 percent of page visits. LCP breaks into four sequential subparts that sum to the total: Time to First Byte (TTFB), the time until the first bytes of the HTML response arrive, typically around 40 percent of LCP; Resource Load Delay, the gap between TTFB and when the browser starts loading the LCP resource, ideally under 10 percent of LCP; Resource Load Duration, the time to transfer the LCP resource over the network, typically around 40 percent of LCP; and Element Render Delay, the time from resource completion until the LCP element is fully rendered, ideally under 10 percent of LCP.

## Eliminate Resource Load Delay

The single most important rule: never lazy-load your LCP image, because that always adds unnecessary resource load delay and hurts LCP. Make the LCP resource discoverable in the initial HTML response so the browser's preload scanner can find it early. For resources referenced only from CSS or JavaScript, use link rel=preload with fetchpriority=high. Apply fetchpriority=high directly on the img element that is likely to be the LCP so the browser prioritizes it.

## Eliminate Element Render Delay

Keep the render-blocking stylesheet smaller than the LCP resource so styles do not become the bottleneck. Avoid synchronous scripts in the head that block rendering. Consider server-side rendering so the image is present in the HTML and does not depend on JavaScript to appear.

## Reduce Resource Load Duration

Optimize images and serve modern formats, deliver assets from a content delivery network close to the user, and use appropriate cache-control policies so repeat visits are fast. Because TTFB and Resource Load Duration together account for roughly 80 percent of LCP, server response and network transfer are where most LCP wins come from.

title: web.dev (Google), Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
text:
## What INP Measures

INP assesses a page's overall responsiveness to user interactions by observing the latency of all click, tap, and keyboard interactions that occur throughout the lifespan of a user's visit to a page, and reporting a single representative value (close to the worst). Only clicking with a mouse, tapping a touchscreen, and pressing a key count. Scrolling, hovering, and zooming are explicitly excluded because they are not discrete interactions with a next paint.

## Thresholds

An INP of 200 milliseconds or less is Good. An INP greater than 200 ms and less than or equal to 500 ms Needs Improvement. An INP greater than 500 ms is Poor. As with all Core Web Vitals, evaluate at the 75th percentile of interactions.

## The Three Phases of an Interaction

Every interaction has three sequential parts. Input Delay is the time before the event handler callbacks begin executing, often caused by long tasks blocking the main thread. Processing Duration is the time for all the event handler callbacks to run to completion. Presentation Delay is the time after the callbacks finish until the browser paints the next frame that reflects the interaction.

## Blocking the Main Thread

Long tasks are a primary cause of input delay: while the main thread is busy running a long task, it cannot start the interaction's event handlers, so the user waits. To improve INP, break up long tasks, yield to the main thread, defer non-critical work, and minimize the work done inside event handlers so the next paint can happen quickly. The main thread is single-threaded; anything that monopolizes it delays every pending interaction.

title: web.dev (Google), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
text:
## What CLS Measures

CLS is a measure of the largest burst of layout shift scores for every unexpected layout shift that occurs during the entire lifecycle of a page. A layout shift happens any time a visible element changes its start position between two frames without a user interaction to explain it. A good CLS is 0.1 or less; 0.1 to 0.25 Needs Improvement; above 0.25 is Poor. Evaluate at the 75th percentile across mobile and desktop.

## The Layout Shift Score Formula

layout shift score = impact fraction x distance fraction. The impact fraction is the proportion of the viewport area affected by the unstable elements across the two frames. The distance fraction is the greatest distance any unstable element moves, horizontally or vertically, divided by the viewport's largest dimension. Multiplying the two rewards small, contained movement and punishes large elements jumping far.

## Session Windows

Rather than summing every shift over the whole page life, CLS uses session windows. A session window is a burst of shifts separated by gaps of less than 1 second, capped at a maximum window length of 5 seconds. CLS reports the single session window with the highest total score, so one very unstable moment dominates the metric rather than being diluted.

## Common Causes and Fixes

The usual causes are images or videos without width and height attributes (or a set aspect-ratio), ads, embeds, and iframes that resize dynamically without reserved space, web fonts causing a flash of unstyled or re-sized text, and DOM injected above existing content in response to a network response. Fixes: always include size attributes or CSS aspect-ratio on media so the browser reserves the box before load, reserve space for late-arriving content, and prefer transform animations, which do not trigger layout shifts, over animating layout-affecting properties like top or height.

title: MDN Web Docs, Critical rendering path
text:
## What the Critical Rendering Path Is

The critical rendering path is the sequence of steps the browser goes through to convert HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into pixels on the screen: DOM construction, CSSOM construction, render tree construction, layout (reflow), and paint. Optimizing it improves render performance and keeps reflows and repaints running at 60 frames per second to prevent jank.

## DOM and CSSOM Construction

DOM construction is incremental: HTML bytes become tokens, tokens become nodes, and nodes are assembled into the DOM tree. More nodes means longer subsequent path events. CSSOM construction is not incremental. CSS is render-blocking: the browser blocks rendering until it has received and processed all CSS, because later rules can override earlier ones, so nothing can be safely painted until the full stylesheet is parsed. Less specific selectors like .foo are marginally faster to match than deeply nested ones like .bar .foo, but the difference is microseconds and should be measured before optimizing.

## Render Tree, Layout, and Paint

The render tree merges the DOM and CSSOM and includes only visible content: the head is excluded, and elements with display: none and their descendants are excluded. Layout (also called reflow) computes the size and position of every element in the render tree; it depends on the number of nodes and is triggered by resizing, orientation change, and render-tree modifications. Layout during scrolling or animation causes jank. Paint fills in pixels; after the first paint only the impacted areas are repainted.

## JavaScript Is Parser-Blocking

HTML parsing halts when the parser encounters a script, because the script may alter the DOM; the browser must download and execute it before continuing, unless the script is marked async or defer. To optimize the path, minimize the number of critical resources (defer or async non-critical assets), reduce request size through minification, split non-critical CSS into media-query-scoped non-blocking requests, and prioritize the load order of critical assets to shorten the path.

title: MDN Web Docs, Basic concepts of flexbox
text:
## One-Dimensional Layout and the Two Axes

Flexbox (Flexible Box Layout) is a one-dimensional layout model that distributes space between items along a single axis at a time, either a row or a column, in contrast to Grid, which is two-dimensional. Setting display: flex on an element makes it a flex container and its direct children flex items. The main axis is set by flex-direction (row, row-reverse, column, column-reverse); the cross axis runs perpendicular to it. With flex-direction: row the main axis is horizontal and the cross axis vertical; with column they swap.

## Container Properties

flex-direction sets the main axis direction. flex-wrap controls whether items wrap onto multiple lines (default nowrap; wrap lets items flow to new lines). flex-flow is the shorthand for flex-direction and flex-wrap. justify-content distributes space along the main axis with values flex-start (default), flex-end, center, space-between, space-around, and space-evenly. align-items aligns items along the cross axis with stretch (default), flex-start, flex-end, center, and baseline. align-content distributes wrapped lines along the cross axis. align-self overrides align-items for a single item.

## Item Properties and the flex Shorthand

Each item has three sizing properties. flex-grow (default 0) controls how much an item grows relative to siblings when there is free space. flex-shrink (default 1) controls how much it shrinks when there is not enough space. flex-basis (default auto) sets the item's size before free space is distributed. The flex shorthand combines all three in the order grow, shrink, basis. Useful keywords: flex: initial equals 0 1 auto (items do not grow but can shrink); flex: auto equals 1 1 auto (grow and shrink); flex: none equals 0 0 auto (fully inflexible); flex: 1 equals 1 1 0 (proportional growth from a zero basis, the common equal-columns pattern). Use the gap property to space items rather than margins.

title: MDN Web Docs, Basic concepts of grid layout
text:
## Two-Dimensional Layout

CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system of intersecting horizontal and vertical lines that define rows and columns at the same time, unlike flexbox which lays out along a single axis. Setting display: grid or display: inline-grid on an element makes it a grid container and its direct children grid items. Grid is ideal for page-level layout; flexbox excels at one-dimensional component alignment.

## Tracks, Lines, Cells, and Areas

A grid track is the space between two adjacent grid lines, defined with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. Grid lines are numbered, so a three-column grid has four column lines; items are placed with grid-column and grid-row using a start / end syntax, for example grid-column: 1 / 4 spans from line 1 to line 4. A grid cell is the smallest unit, the intersection of one row and one column. A grid area is a rectangle spanning one or more cells, which can be named with grid-template-areas and assigned to items with grid-area.

## The fr Unit, repeat(), and minmax()

The fr unit represents a fraction of the available space: grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr makes three equal columns, and 2fr 1fr 1fr makes the first twice as wide. repeat() shortens repetitive definitions, so repeat(3, 1fr) equals 1fr 1fr 1fr and repeat(12, 1fr) builds a twelve-column grid. minmax(min, max) sets a floor and ceiling for a track, for example grid-auto-rows: minmax(100px, auto) makes rows at least 100px but able to grow. Combining repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) produces a responsive grid with no media queries.

## Explicit vs Implicit Grid and Gaps

The explicit grid is what you define with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows; when items overflow it, an implicit grid is generated automatically, sized by grid-auto-rows and grid-auto-columns. Spacing between tracks uses gap (shorthand for row-gap and column-gap), which replaces the old margin hacks for gutters.

title: MDN Web Docs, Specificity
text:
## The Three-Column Model

Specificity is the weight the cascade uses to pick which competing declaration applies, and it is only considered after origin and importance. It is expressed as ID, CLASS, TYPE (written like 1-0-0). The ID column counts ID selectors such as #example (1-0-0 each). The CLASS column counts class selectors like .myClass, attribute selectors like [type=radio], and pseudo-classes like :hover and :nth-of-type() (0-1-0 each). The TYPE column counts type selectors like p and h1 and pseudo-elements like ::before (0-0-1 each). Columns are compared left to right: an ID always beats any number of classes, and a class always beats any number of types.

## Zero-Weight and Special Selectors

The universal selector * and the :where() pseudo-class contribute 0-0-0. Combinators (+, >, ~, the descendant space) add no weight. :is(), :not(), and :has() add no weight themselves, but take the specificity of their most specific argument, so :is(p, #fakeId) counts as 1-0-0. :where() always forces its contents to 0-0-0, which is the tool for writing far-reaching selectors that stay easy to override, especially for third-party CSS.

## Inline Styles, !important, and Ties

Inline style attributes behave like a fourth, highest column (1-0-0-0) and can only be overridden by !important. When specificity ties, source order wins: the last matching declaration is applied. A declaration marked !important overrides any normal declaration in the same layer and origin regardless of specificity, which reverses the usual cascade.

## Anti-Pattern: Specificity Wars

Overusing !important and high-specificity selectors (especially IDs) leads to specificity wars: an escalating cycle where each new rule needs an even higher specificity to override the last, producing brittle, unmaintainable CSS. The recommended discipline is to keep specificity flat and low, prefer classes and attribute selectors over IDs, use cascade layers (@layer) instead of !important to control precedence, and use :where() to add reach without adding weight. Never duplicate a selector like #id#id#id to win a fight.

title: MDN Web Docs, CSS container queries
text:
## Styling Based on a Container, Not the Viewport

Container queries let you apply styles based on the size of a containing element rather than the viewport, which makes a component responsive to its context and reusable anywhere on the page. This is the key difference from media queries: a media query reacts to the browser window, so a component must know where it is placed, while a container query lets the same card adapt whether it sits in a wide main column or a narrow sidebar.

## Setting Up a Query Container

Declare a containment context with container-type. inline-size queries the container's inline (width) dimension and is the common case; size queries both inline and block dimensions; normal disables size queries but still allows style queries. container-name gives the context a name for targeted queries, and the container shorthand combines name and type as container: sidebar / inline-size. You then write @container (width > 700px) { ... } for an unnamed nearest container, or @container sidebar (width > 700px) { ... } to target a named one.

## Container Query Units

Container query length units are relative to the queried container: cqw is 1 percent of container width, cqh is 1 percent of container height, cqi is 1 percent of container inline size, cqb is 1 percent of container block size, and cqmin and cqmax are the smaller and larger of cqi and cqb. Example: inside @container (width > 700px), font-size: max(1.5em, 1.23em + 2cqi) scales type with the container. A component styled with container queries and container units can be dropped into any layout and respond correctly without global breakpoints.

title: MDN Web Docs, CSS logical properties and values
text:
## Flow-Relative, Not Physical

Logical properties and values define layout relative to the content's writing direction (block and inline flow) rather than physical directions (top, right, bottom, left). The inline dimension runs parallel to the flow of text within a line; the block dimension runs perpendicular to it. In a horizontal left-to-right language like English, inline is horizontal and block is vertical; in a vertical writing mode like Japanese, they swap. Writing code in logical terms means one stylesheet adapts to left-to-right, right-to-left (Arabic, Hebrew), and vertical scripts without change.

## The Logical Property Set

Sizing uses inline-size (replacing width) and block-size (replacing height), plus min- and max- variants. Spacing uses margin-inline and margin-block (and the -start and -end long forms), and padding-inline and padding-block similarly. Borders use border-inline and border-block plus corner radii like border-start-start-radius. Positioning uses the inset shorthand and inset-inline-start, inset-inline-end, inset-block-start, inset-block-end in place of top, right, bottom, left. Flow-relative values such as inline-start, inline-end, block-start, block-end, start, and end replace physical keywords in properties like text-align and float.

## Why Prefer Them

Using margin-inline-start instead of margin-left means a right-to-left layout automatically mirrors, so you avoid the classic bug of a hard-coded left margin that looks wrong in Arabic. Logical properties are the modern default: more semantic, internationalization-ready, and they work seamlessly with writing-mode, direction, and text-orientation.

title: MDN Web Docs, Responsive design
text:
## Mobile-First and the Viewport Meta Tag

Responsive design is an approach, not a technology: one document serves all screen sizes by reflowing rather than shipping separate mobile and desktop sites. The recommended practice is mobile-first: build the simple single-column narrow-screen layout first, then progressively add multi-column layout for wider screens as space allows. Every responsive page must include the viewport meta tag, meta name=viewport content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1", which tells mobile browsers to use the device width instead of a fixed default (around 980px on iPhone), without which responsive CSS does not take effect.

## Media Queries and Content-Based Breakpoints

Media queries apply CSS conditionally, for example @media screen and (width >= 80rem). Breakpoints are the widths where the layout changes. Best practice is to define breakpoints in relative units and choose them based on where your content breaks, not by targeting specific device sizes, because the device landscape changes constantly and content-driven breakpoints age better. Modern layout methods, flexbox and grid, are inherently responsive and make fluid grids straightforward, with the fr unit distributing space proportionally.

## Responsive Media and Typography

Set img, picture, and video to max-width: 100% so media never overflows its container. Use the srcset and sizes attributes to let the browser pick an appropriately sized image for the device and avoid downloading oversized files, and use the picture element for art direction (serving a different crop or format per viewport). For type, scale with media queries or fluidly with calc(), for example font-size: calc(1.5rem + 4vw); never use a bare vw unit for font-size because it disables user zoom, which is an accessibility failure. Combining a rem base with a vw term keeps text both fluid and zoomable.

title: MDN Web Docs, JavaScript execution model (event loop)
text:
## Call Stack, Job Queue, and the Event Loop

A JavaScript agent (analogous to a thread) has a heap for objects, a call stack of execution contexts, and a job queue (the event loop). The call stack is last-in-first-out: each function call pushes an execution context and returns pop it. The agent repeatedly pulls a job from the queue and executes it; a running job may enqueue more jobs, which are added to the end of the queue.

## Run-to-Completion

JavaScript uses run-to-completion semantics: each job executes completely before any other job starts, and a running function cannot be preempted. This makes ordering predictable. Given two promise.then callbacks that each increment and log a shared counter, the output is guaranteed to be 1 then 2, because the first callback runs entirely before the second begins. The upside is easy reasoning; the downside is that a job that takes too long freezes everything.

## Microtasks vs Tasks

Jobs are not all equal priority. The HTML event loop splits jobs into tasks (macrotasks) and microtasks, and the microtask queue is fully drained before the next task is pulled. Microtasks are higher priority and include promise .then, .catch, and .finally handlers and queueMicrotask(). Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, and UI rendering. This is why a chain of resolved promises runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0) queued at the same time.

## Do Not Block the Main Thread

Because execution is single-threaded and run-to-completion, a long synchronous job stops the browser from handling clicks, scroll, events, and rendering, which is the source of the "a script is taking too long to run" dialog. The best practice is to keep job processing short and, when a computation is large, cut it into several smaller jobs, yielding to the event loop between them (for example with await or setTimeout) so user interactions and paints can happen in between. Asynchronous platform APIs like fetch and IndexedDB use events and callbacks precisely so the app stays responsive while waiting.

title: React (react.dev), Rules of Hooks
text:
## Rule 1: Only Call Hooks at the Top Level

Do not call Hooks inside loops, conditions, nested functions, or try/catch/finally blocks. Always call Hooks at the top level of your React function, before any early returns. Valid places are the top level of a function component's body and the top level of a custom Hook's body. Invalid places include inside conditions or loops, after a conditional return, in event handlers, in class components, and inside functions passed to useMemo, useReducer, or useEffect. React relies on the call order of Hooks to keep their state associated correctly across renders, so calling them conditionally or in loops corrupts that ordering and produces wrong state.

## Rule 2: Only Call Hooks from React Functions

Do not call Hooks from ordinary JavaScript functions. Call them only from React function components or from custom Hooks (functions whose names start with use). Following this rule keeps all of a component's stateful logic visible from its source and lets React and tooling reason about it.

## Custom Hooks

The two rules also apply to custom Hooks, which are simply JavaScript functions whose names start with use and which call other Hooks. Naming a function with the use prefix is what signals to React and to the linter that it may contain Hook calls and must obey the rules; a plain helper function must not call Hooks. Custom Hooks let you extract and share stateful logic between components without sharing state itself.

## Enforcement

These rules are not stylistic; violating them breaks React's internal bookkeeping. Because React tracks each Hook only by the order in which it is called on every render, a Hook that is sometimes skipped (inside an if, an early return, or a loop) shifts every later Hook's slot and corrupts state. Use the eslint-plugin-react-hooks plugin to catch violations automatically rather than relying on discipline, and keep Hook calls unconditional at the very top of the component.

title: React (react.dev), Rendering Lists and Keys
text:
## Why Keys Exist

Keys tell React which array item each rendered component corresponds to, so React can match items between renders even when they move, get inserted, or get deleted. The analogy: files in a folder have names rather than being referred to by position, because once you delete one, positions shift and become confusing. A well-chosen key provides more information than the position in the array; even if the position changes due to reordering, the key lets React identify the item throughout its lifetime.

## The Rules of Keys

Keys must be unique among siblings (the same key value may be reused across different arrays). Keys must not change between renders, or they defeat their purpose, so do not generate them while rendering. For data from a database, use the database IDs, which are unique by nature; for locally created data, use an incrementing counter, crypto.randomUUID(), or a uuid package at creation time.

## Anti-Patterns

Do not use an item's array index as its key. React falls back to the index when you provide no key, but because the render order changes when an item is inserted, deleted, or the array is reordered, index-as-key leads to subtle and confusing bugs (wrong item state, stale form inputs). Do not generate keys on the fly such as key={Math.random()}: the keys never match between renders, so React recreates every component and DOM node each render, which is slow and destroys any user input inside the list items. Use a stable ID based on the data instead. Note that a component does not receive key as a prop; if it needs the id, pass it separately, for example Profile key={id} userId={id}.

title: React (react.dev), useMemo, Should you add useMemo everywhere?
text:
## Should You Add useMemo Everywhere?

No. If most interactions in your app are coarse (replacing a whole page or section), memoization is usually unnecessary; if they are granular (dragging shapes in a drawing editor), it can help a lot. useMemo is valuable in only a few cases: the calculation is noticeably slow and its dependencies rarely change; you pass the value as a prop to a component wrapped in memo and want to skip re-rendering when it is unchanged; or the value is used as a dependency of another Hook such as useMemo or useEffect. There is no benefit to wrapping a calculation in useMemo in other cases, and no significant harm either, but memoizing everything makes code less readable, and not all memoization is effective: a single value that is always new is enough to break memoization for an entire component.

## How to Tell If a Calculation Is Expensive

Unless you are creating or looping over thousands of objects, it is probably not expensive. To be sure, measure with console.time('filter array') ... console.timeEnd('filter array') around the code, perform the interaction, and read the logged time. If the total adds up to a significant amount, say 1ms or more, it might make sense to memoize. React advises relying on useMemo only as a performance optimization: if your code does not work without it, find and fix the underlying bug first, then add useMemo for speed.

## Reduce the Need for Memoization

Most memoization can be avoided by design. Let a wrapper component accept JSX as children so its children do not re-render when it updates its own state. Prefer local state and do not lift state higher than necessary. Keep rendering logic pure; if re-rendering causes a visible artifact, that is a bug to fix, not to paper over with memoization. Avoid unnecessary Effects that update state, since most React performance problems come from chains of Effect-triggered renders. Often it is simpler to move an object or function inside an Effect, or outside the component, than to memoize it.

title: React (react.dev), You Might Not Need an Effect
text:
## Two Cases That Do Not Need Effects

You do not need an Effect to transform data for rendering, and you do not need an Effect to handle user events. Using an Effect to compute derived data forces an extra render pass: React renders with stale data, commits to the DOM, runs the Effect which sets state, then re-renders from scratch. Instead, calculate the value at the top level during rendering. The canonical example: rather than a fullName state synced by an Effect from firstName and lastName, just write const fullName = firstName + ' ' + lastName during render. The general principle: if something can be calculated from existing props or state, do not put it in state, calculate it during rendering.

## Derived State and Expensive Calculations

Do not mirror props or state into new state kept in sync by an Effect (const [visibleTodos, setVisibleTodos] plus an Effect calling setVisibleTodos). Compute it during render: const visibleTodos = getFilteredTodos(todos, filter). If that calculation is genuinely expensive, wrap it in useMemo, not in an Effect plus state. To reset all state when a prop changes, pass a different key to the component (key={userId}) so React treats it as a new instance, rather than resetting fields in an Effect. To adjust some state when a prop changes, prefer computing derived state during render, for example const selection = items.find(i => i.id === selectedId) ?? null.

## Avoid Chains of Effects and Event Logic in Effects

Do not build chains of Effects where one Effect's state update triggers another Effect's state update; this causes repeated re-render cascades that are the top source of React performance problems. Compute the whole next state in the event handler instead. And do not put event-specific logic in an Effect: showing an 'Added to cart' notification belongs in the click handler, because an Effect runs after render and has lost the context of what the user did. The test: ask why the code needs to run. If it should run because the component was displayed, it belongs in an Effect (synchronizing with an external system, subscriptions, some data fetching with cleanup); if it should run because the user did something specific, it belongs in an event handler.

title: React (react.dev), Sharing State Between Components (controlled vs uncontrolled)
text:
## Lifting State Up

When two components should always change together, remove the state from both, move it to their closest common parent, and pass it down through props with event handlers. The three steps: remove state from the children, pass hardcoded data down from the parent, then add real state to the parent and pass it down along with the setters. This centralizes coordination in one owner.

## Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components

A component with its own local state is uncontrolled: it manages itself with useState and the parent cannot influence it. It is easier to use with less configuration, but harder to coordinate with siblings. A component whose important information is driven by props rather than its own local state is controlled: the parent fully specifies its behavior through props, which is maximally flexible but requires the parent to configure it. These are not strict technical terms but a useful lens; in practice each component mixes some local state and some props. When you build a reusable component, decide deliberately which information is controlled (via props) and which is uncontrolled (local state).

## Single Source of Truth

For each unique piece of state, choose exactly one component to own it. State does not all live in one place; rather, each piece has a specific owning component. Instead of duplicating shared state across components, lift it to the common parent and pass it down. As the app evolves, moving state up or down to find where it belongs is a normal part of development.

title: MDN Web Docs, prefers-reduced-motion
text:
## What It Is and Why It Matters

The prefers-reduced-motion CSS media feature detects whether the user has turned on a system setting to minimize non-essential motion. It exists because animation can trigger discomfort for users with vestibular motion disorders: scaling, panning, and other large-object motion are vestibular triggers that can cause real distress. Respecting this preference is an accessibility requirement, not a nicety, and it maps to WCAG success criteria on motion.

## Values and Usage

The feature has two values. no-preference means the user has expressed no preference and evaluates as false. reduce means the user has enabled reduced motion and evaluates as true, so @media (prefers-reduced-motion) is equivalent to @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce). The pattern is to define your motion normally, then inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) replace or remove the motion, for example swapping a scaling pulse keyframe animation for a gentle opacity dissolve, or setting animation and transition durations to near zero. A common robust default is to author the reduced experience so essential feedback (like state change) remains but large motion is dropped. The feature is Baseline widely available, supported across browsers since January 2020.

## Practical Guidance

The preference comes from an operating system setting (Reduce Motion on macOS and iOS, Show animations off or a similar toggle on Windows and Android), so honoring it respects a choice the user already made system-wide rather than asking again. Because reduce is meant to remove non-essential motion, apply it to large parallax, autoplaying carousels, zoom and slide transitions, and smooth-scroll, while keeping small, non-vestibular cues like opacity fades that communicate state. The feature can also be evaluated in JavaScript through window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') so scripted animations, canvas, and libraries can check the same signal and reduce their motion accordingly. Treat reduced motion as a first-class variant of the design, not an afterthought, so that motion-sensitive users get a safe, still-usable interface.

title: MDN Web Docs, Progressive enhancement
text:
## Definition

Progressive enhancement is a design philosophy that provides a baseline of essential content and functionality to as many users as possible, while delivering the best possible experience only to users of the most modern browsers that can run all the required code. The word progressive means the design achieves a simpler but still usable experience for users of older browsers and limited devices, while progressing the experience up to a more compelling, fully featured experience for users of newer, richer browsers.

## Contrast With Graceful Degradation

Graceful degradation is related but not the same, and is often seen as going in the opposite direction. Progressive enhancement builds up from a working baseline; graceful degradation starts from a full-featured experience and ensures it degrades acceptably on weaker environments. Both approaches are valid and can complement one another. The practical layering: start with semantic HTML content that works with no CSS or JavaScript, add CSS for presentation, then add JavaScript for enhanced behavior, so that if a layer fails the ones beneath still function.

## Techniques and Accessibility

Two supporting techniques are feature detection, used to decide whether a browser can handle more modern functionality, and polyfills, used to add missing features with JavaScript. Special notice should be taken of accessibility: acceptable alternatives should be provided where possible. Because the baseline is real HTML that works without scripts, progressive enhancement inherently keeps core functionality available to assistive technology, search crawlers, and users on flaky networks, which is why it produces more resilient sites than a JavaScript-only approach.

title: web.dev (Google), Browser-level image lazy loading
text:
## The loading Attribute

Browser-level lazy loading defers offscreen images with a single attribute: img src=... loading="lazy" alt=... width=200 height=200. The lazy value defers loading of the resource until it reaches a calculated distance from the viewport; the default eager loads the image regardless of its position. Iframes support the same loading attribute to defer offscreen embeds.

## Do Not Lazy-Load Above-the-Fold or LCP Images

The key caveat: never lazy-load images that are likely to be in the viewport when the page loads, and especially not the Largest Contentful Paint image. Deferred images load more slowly because the browser cannot compute their position until layout completes, so lazy-loading a hero or LCP image directly harms LCP. Lazy loading is for below-the-fold content only.

## Always Set Width and Height

Always specify width and height (or a CSS aspect-ratio) on lazy-loaded images. Without dimensions the image box defaults toward 0 by 0 until the file arrives, which causes Cumulative Layout Shift as surrounding content jumps when the image finally loads. Reserving the box up front keeps the layout stable. Together these rules, eager and prioritized for the LCP image, lazy for offscreen images, sized boxes everywhere, balance fast loading against visual stability.

title: MDN Web Docs, HTML: A good basis for accessibility
text:
## Native Controls Give You Accessibility for Free

Native HTML buttons have default styling (which you will usually override) and built-in keyboard accessibility: users can Tab between buttons and activate them with Space, Return, or Enter. You get this behavior for free just by using the appropriate element. Native elements are also easier to develop with, lighter and more responsive on mobile, and better for SEO. The core principle is the right element for the right job.

## Anti-Pattern: Fake Buttons Built From Divs

Building a control from a generic element, like a div with a click handler acting as a button, throws away all of that. To claw the accessibility back you must add tabindex="0" to make it focusable, role="button" so assistive tech announces it, and JavaScript to handle the Enter and Space keys (for example a keydown handler that calls click() when e.key is Enter), plus visible focus styling. As the guide concludes, this is a lot of extra hassle to build the functionality back in, and there are bound to be other problems with it: better to just use the right element for the right job in the first place. Div soup with onClick handlers is the classic front-end accessibility failure.

## Text Alternatives and Meaningful Link Text

Images need an alt attribute that is a direct, concise representation of what the image conveys and is not duplicated in surrounding text; purely decorative images take an empty alt="" so screen readers skip them (omitting alt entirely makes some screen readers read the filename). Link text must make sense out of context, because screen reader users often pull up a list of links: write Find out more about whales, not click here. Associate every form control with a label via for and id, which lets screen readers announce the field and lets sighted users click the label to focus the input.

title: W3C, Understanding WCAG 2.2, SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A)
text:
## Success Criterion 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A)

All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes, except where the underlying function requires input that depends on the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints. In plain terms: anything a mouse user can do, a keyboard user must be able to do too, with the narrow exception of inherently path-dependent input like freehand drawing.

## Intent

The criterion ensures content is operable by keyboard or keyboard-alternate devices. It benefits people with no vision, people using speech input or on-screen keyboards (which emulate a keyboard), and low-vision users who struggle to track a pointer. Path-dependence is the dividing line: resizing a window or moving an object to a target has endpoints a keyboard can express, whereas the exact stroke of freehand drawing does not, so only the truly path-dependent case is exempt.

## Relationship to No Keyboard Trap (2.1.2)

SC 2.1.1 requires keyboard operability; the companion SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap requires that keyboard focus can always move away from a component using only the keyboard, so a user who tabs into a widget can tab back out. For a UI engineer this means every custom interactive component must be reachable by Tab, operable with the expected keys for its role, and escapable, and must show a visible focus indicator, or it fails at Level A, the minimum conformance level.

title: React (react.dev), Thinking in React
text:
## Step 1: Break the UI Into a Component Hierarchy

Draw boxes around every component and subcomponent in the mockup and name them. Apply the single responsibility principle: a component should ideally do one thing; if it grows, decompose it into smaller subcomponents. A well-structured data model tends to map one-to-one onto the component tree, so each component matches one piece of your data.

## Step 2: Build a Static Version First

Build a version that renders the UI from the data model using only props and component composition, with no interactivity. Do not use state at all for the static version. State is reserved only for interactivity, data that changes over time. You can build top-down or bottom-up; for simple UIs top-down is usually easier.

## Step 3: Find the Minimal Complete Representation of State

State is the minimal set of changing data your app needs to remember; keep it DRY and compute everything else on demand. For each piece of data, ask three questions. Does it remain unchanged over time? Then it is not state. Is it passed in from a parent via props? Then it is not state. Can you compute it from existing state or props? Then it is definitely not state. What remains is state. For a searchable product table, the product list is not state (props), the search text and checkbox are state, and the filtered list is not state because it is computed from the list plus the search text plus the checkbox. Storing derived data like the filtered list in state is the classic redundant-state bug.

## Steps 4 and 5: Where State Lives and Inverse Data Flow

For each piece of state, find every component that uses it, find their closest common parent, and put the state there (or in a component above it, or a new component created just to hold it). Because React uses one-way data flow down the tree, to let a deep child change parent state you add inverse data flow: pass setter functions down as props and call them from the child's onChange handlers. This keeps a single source of truth while making updates explicit.

title: web.dev (Google), Optimize long tasks
text:
## What a Long Task Is

A long task is any discrete piece of work that runs on the browser's main thread for longer than 50 milliseconds; the portion beyond 50 ms is the task's blocking period. Long tasks harm responsiveness because the browser blocks interactions from occurring while any task is running, so a long task makes the interface feel unresponsive and directly worsens Interaction to Next Paint (INP). Because the main thread is single-threaded, one long task delays every pending click, tap, keypress, and paint.

## Yield to the Main Thread

The fix is to break long tasks into smaller chunks and yield to the main thread between them, so the browser can service higher-priority work, including user interactions, much sooner. The classic technique defers work with setTimeout(fn, 0), which queues the rest as a new task; a caveat is that after five nested setTimeout calls the browser imposes a minimum 5 ms delay. The purpose-built API is scheduler.yield(), awaited inside async code as await scheduler.yield(); it returns a promise and provides prioritized continuation, meaning the remainder of the current task resumes before other similar tasks start, with a setTimeout-based fallback for browsers that lack it.

## Batch, and What Not to Use

Rather than yielding after every operation, batch work and yield only when you have exceeded a deadline, commonly 50 ms, to avoid creating new long tasks. isInputPending() is no longer recommended, because it can incorrectly return false even after a user has interacted and it ignores non-input work like animations that also need responsiveness. Other structural tools include code splitting to reduce script execution and moving heavy pure computation off the main thread into a web worker. The guiding principle: do user-facing work such as UI updates first, defer lower-priority background work, and always yield so interactions can interleave.
